newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-EDBERG BOWS OUT TO FELLOW SWEDE ENQVIST.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-EDBERG BOWS OUT TO FELLOW SWEDE ENQVIST.

text.p: Stefan Edberg made an emotional exit from the Paris Open and competitive tennis outside his own country when he was beaten 6-4 7-6 by fellow Swede Thomas Enqvist in the quarter-finals on Friday.

Edberg, who retires after next weeks' Stockholm Open and the Davis Cup final at home to France, was presented with a miniature replica of the Paris Open trophy he won in 1990 and bowed to a cheering crowd before walking off centre court.

"The Paris crowd have always been behind me. It was great playing here even if I didn't win the match," said Edberg after the crowd urged him on in a tense second set tiebreak that went to Enqvist 8-6.
Number 12 seed Enqvist meets compatriot Magnus Gustafsson in one semifinal on Saturday with Yevgeny Kafelnikov, the highest surviving seed at number four, against qualifier Petr Korda in the other.
French Open champion Kafelnikov, who will move up to world number three in ATP Monday's rankings, beat Dutchman Paul Haarhuis in straight sets 7-6 6-1.
Czech veteran Korda, playing his ninth match of the Bercy tournament, eliminated French hope Arnaud Boetsch 7-6 7-6.
Gustafsson beat 1994 runner-up Marc Rosset of Switzerland, second round conqueror of top seed Pete Sampras, 6-2 3-6 6-2.
The last time only two seeds reached the quarter-finals was in 1988 -- American defending champion Tim Mayotte and Russia's Andrei Chesnokov.
Edberg said he thought his match was of a very high quality with both he and Enqvist playing well.
"It was sad to lose in the tiebreak, it would have been nice to go to a third set," said the 30-year-old Edberg.
"I'm disappointed. It was a great opportunity here this week with lots of seeds going out.

"But I knew today would be tough. I did what could but it wasn't enough. Thomas played extremely well. I thought he'd be a little tighter, but he didn't let anything bother him, not even the crowd. He hardly made any mistakes."
Enqvist came back from 5-2 down in the tiebreak and won with his second match point when Edberg, on his own serve, netted his opponent's return.

Veteran 1992 French Open finalist Korda, coming back after nearly quitting tennis last year because of injury, said: "After the U.S. Open I locked myself inside the hall and just worked, you know, hitting balls, serving, hitting balls, serving, just like that every day.

"Suddenly I started to play well in Ostrava. Unfortunately, I couldn't play (in Stuttgart) last week because I didn't make time for qualifying because I was in the final in Ostrava," added Korda, who last had to qualify in Vienna in 1989.

Boetsch, who played brilliantly in eliminating second seed Michael Chang 6-1 6-3 in the third round on Thursday night, was well-placed to take the first set when he led 6-5 with his own serve to come.
Instead, Korda, ranked five places below Boetsch at 37, broke back and won the set 7-2 in the tiebreak.
Boetsch said: "I felt a little heavier than yesterday. He played very well and gave me a lot of trouble with his left-handed serve."
At 5-5 in the second set tiebreak, Korda double faulted to give Boestch another chance to serve for a set. But the Czech saved the point with a fine passing shot.

Fortune favoured the more adventurous, less nervous Korda and a net cord ball that dropped in Frenchman's court gave him the chance to serve for the match, taking the tiebreak 8-6 when Boetsch netted a return.
"It's true he had the luck, but in the second set I led 3-1, 4-2 and served for the set. I should have sewn it up," Boetsch said.
Korda made more unforced errors, but he also had far more winning shots.

Gustafsson, who upset Andre Agassi in the second round, overcame a net cord controversy that upset him in the second set when the detector for serves sounded during a rally that he won and, first the umpire, then the referee ordered the point to be replayed.
"In all the years I've been playing, if there was confusion over a point play was stopped, but here it wasn't. I was upset when they said we had to replay the point," Gustafsson said.
"We both started to play worse tennis. It destroyed the rhythm of the match."
The detector sounded several times during the set before being turned off. It was adjusted for the third.
